case_studies.title: TSCG: Deterministic Tool-Schema Compilation for Agentic LLM Deployments
case_studies.abstract: Production agent frameworks (OpenAI Function Calling, Anthropic Tool Use, MCP) transmit tool schemas as JSON, a format designed for machine parsing, not for interpretation by language models. For small models (4B-14B), this protocol mismatch accounts for the majority of tool-use failure at production catalog sizes. We present TSCG, a deterministic tool-schema compiler that resolves this mismatch at the API boundary, converting JSON schemas into token-efficient structured text without model access, fine-tuning, or runtime search. TSCG combines eight composable operators with a formal compressio
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of tool-schema compilation for large language models by building a deterministic tool-schema compiler called TSCG, which converts JSON schemas into token-efficient structured text, resulting in improved tool-use success rates. TSCG achieves this without requiring model access, fine-tuning, or runtime search. This innovation has the potential to enhance the performance of production agent frameworks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage large language model deployments, here is what to do: review your current tool-schema compilation process, consider integrating TSCG to improve token efficiency, and assess the potential benefits for your production catalog sizes.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novel AI solution (TSCG) directly applicable to IT engineers working with large language models (LLM) in production. Compiling JSON schemas into interpretable text resolves tool-use failures at the API boundary, a common issue in LLM deployments. IT engineers could use this to streamline LLM tooling, reducing errors and improving model performance. This has potential for immediate real-world impact and can be monetised through improved model efficiency and reduced deployment costs.

case_studies.title: UniPool: A Globally Shared Expert Pool for Mixture-of-Experts
case_studies.abstract: Modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures allocate expert capacity through a rigid per-layer rule: each transformer layer owns a separate expert set. This convention couples depth scaling with linear expert-parameter growth and assumes that every layer needs isolated expert capacity. However, recent analyses and our routing probe challenge this allocation rule: replacing a deeper layer's learned top-k router with uniform random routing drops downstream accuracy by only 1.0-1.6 points across multiple production MoE models. Motivated by this redundancy, we propose UniPool, an MoE architectur
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inefficient expert capacity allocation in Mixture-of-Experts architectures by proposing a new architecture called UniPool, which allows for a globally shared expert pool. The UniPool architecture was built and tested, resulting in a more efficient allocation of expert capacity. This research may not be directly relevant to IT infrastructure work, but could be of interest to those managing cloud infrastructure for AI and machine learning applications.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for AI and machine learning applications, this research may be of interest as it could lead to more efficient use of resources in the future, but it does not require any immediate action: no changes to existing infrastructure are needed at this time, and you can continue to monitor the development of UniPool and similar technologies.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper reveals a surprising concept in AI architecture, relevant to IT systems that use AI, but uncertain value in 90 days as it requires significant expertise in MoE architectures.

case_studies.title: Why Global LLM Leaderboards Are Misleading: Small Portfolios for Heterogeneous Supervised ML
case_studies.abstract: Ranking LLMs via pairwise human feedback underpins current leaderboards for open-ended tasks, such as creative writing and problem-solving. We analyze ~89K comparisons in 116 languages from 52 LLMs from Arena, and show that the best-fit global Bradley-Terry (BT) ranking is misleading. Nearly 2/3 of the decisive votes cancel out, and even the top 50 models according to the global BT ranking are statistically indistinguishable (pairwise win probabilities are at most 0.53 within the top 50 models). We trace this failure to strong, structured heterogeneity of opinions across language, task, and ti
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inaccurate rankings in large language models, building a new analysis of 89K comparisons to show that current leaderboards are misleading, resulting in the finding that even top models are statistically indistinguishable. The researchers analyzed comparisons from 52 language models across 116 languages. The study reveals that the best-fit global ranking is misleading due to heterogeneity of opinions across languages and tasks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the ranking of large language models rather than cloud infrastructure management. If your organization uses large language models for specific tasks, this research may be of interest, but it does not require immediate action. No direct changes to IT infrastructure are needed based on this study.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper presents interesting findings on the limitations of current LLM evaluation methods. While it's not surprising that existing methods can be flawed, the analysis of ~89K comparisons across 116 languages is noteworthy. However, it has low direct relevance to IT infrastructure and engineering, and while it may contribute to the understanding of LLMs, it does not have a high potential for value within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Are We Making Progress in Multimodal Domain Generalization? A Comprehensive Benchmark Study
case_studies.abstract: Despite the growing popularity of Multimodal Domain Generalization (MMDG) for enhancing model robustness, it remains unclear whether reported performance gains reflect genuine algorithmic progress or are artifacts of inconsistent evaluation protocols. Current research is fragmented, with studies varying significantly across datasets, modality configurations, and experimental settings. Furthermore, existing benchmarks focus predominantly on action recognition, often neglecting critical real-world challenges such as input corruptions, missing modalities, and model trustworthiness. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inconsistent evaluation protocols in Multimodal Domain Generalization, building a comprehensive benchmark study to assess model robustness. The result is a clearer understanding of whether performance gains are due to genuine algorithmic progress or experimental artifacts. This is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: Relit-LiVE: Relight Video by Jointly Learning Environment Video
case_studies.abstract: Recent advances have shown that large-scale video diffusion models can be repurposed as neural renderers by first decomposing videos into intrinsic scene representations and then performing forward rendering under novel illumination. While promising, this paradigm fundamentally relies on accurate intrinsic decomposition, which remains highly unreliable for real-world videos and often leads to distorted appearances, broken materials, and accumulated temporal artifacts during relighting. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of unreliable video relighting by introducing Relit-LiVE, a framework that jointly learns environment and video to produce consistent results. The researchers built a novel video relighting framework that reduces distorted appearances and broken materials. The result is a more accurate and physically consistent video relighting process.

case_studies.title: NeuroAgent: LLM Agents for Multimodal Neuroimaging Analysis and Research
case_studies.abstract: Multimodal neuroimaging analysis often involves complex, modality-specific preprocessing workflows that require careful configuration, quality control, and coordination across heterogeneous toolchains. Beyond preprocessing, downstream statistical analysis and disease classification commonly require task-specific code, evaluation protocols, and data-format conventions, creating additional barriers between raw acquisitions and reproducible scientific analysis. We present NeuroAgent, an LLM-driven agentic framework that automates key preprocessing and analysis steps for heterogeneous neuroimaging
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of complex neuroimaging analysis by building an automated framework called NeuroAgent. NeuroAgent uses large language models to automate key preprocessing and analysis steps for neuroimaging data. The result is a more streamlined and reproducible scientific analysis process.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on neuroimaging analysis and research. However, if your organisation uses neuroimaging data, you may want to explore how NeuroAgent can be integrated into your workflows. This would likely require collaboration with the research team or neuroimaging experts.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper describes an LLM-driven framework for neuroimaging analysis, which is not directly relevant to most IT engineers' work. However, the use of LLM agents affects how IT engineers might work with such tools in the future. The paper's value is low for immediate practical application.
